_meta.description: Pest knowledge base for the Smart Pest Detection & Prediction System. Keys match the trained model's class labels (see backend/model/class_names.json). Content compiled from Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture (doa.gov.lk) advisories and general Integrated Pest Management (IPM) references. Intended for advisory use, not a substitute for a certified agronomist.
_meta.classes_source: 12 generic classes from Kaggle 'Agricultural Pests Image Dataset'; 7 Sri Lankan crop-pest classes (brown_planthopper, rice_stem_borer, fall_armyworm, fruit_fly, thrips, mealybug, leafhopper) added from the IP102 dataset.
_meta.sinhala_names_todo: sinhala_name field intentionally omitted until verified with a Sinhala agronomy source; add per class later.
_meta.note_class_names: class_names.json must match whatever model is loaded. The committed model has 12 classes; after retraining with the updated notebook it will have 19. Retrain and replace class_names.json together with pest_model.keras.

damage_symptoms: Ants themselves rarely eat crops, but they farm and protect sap-sucking pests (aphids, mealybugs, scale) for their honeydew.
Presence of ant trails on stems often signals an aphid or mealybug infestation nearby.
Some species disturb roots and seedlings by nesting in the soil around them.
organic_treatments: Control the sap-sucking pests (aphids/mealybugs) the ants are tending — remove the food source and ants leave.
Apply a sticky band (grease/petroleum jelly) around tree trunks to block ants from climbing.
Pour boiling water or a diluted neem solution into accessible ground nests.
Sprinkle wood ash or diatomaceous earth around plant bases.
chemical_treatments: Ant baits containing borax or fipronil placed on trails (targets the colony).
Spot-treat nests with a labelled contact insecticide only if infestation is heavy.
prevention: Keep the field free of honeydew-producing pests.
Remove decaying wood and debris that host nests.
Avoid over-mulching directly against stems.

damage_symptoms: Bees are pollinators and are beneficial — they do not damage healthy crops.
Their presence usually indicates a healthy, flowering, pollinator-friendly field.
organic_treatments: No treatment needed. Do not spray or destroy bees.
If a swarm settles in an unsafe location, contact a local beekeeper to relocate it — do not exterminate.
chemical_treatments: None. Avoid spraying insecticides during flowering and daytime foraging hours to protect bees.
prevention: Encourage bees for better pollination and yield.
Spray any necessary pesticides in the late evening when bees are not foraging, and never on open flowers.

damage_symptoms: Irregular holes chewed in leaves, sometimes leaving only the leaf veins (skeletonised leaves).
Damage to flowers, fruits and stems depending on species.
Larvae (grubs) of some beetles feed on roots underground, causing wilting.
organic_treatments: Hand-pick adult beetles in the early morning and drop them into soapy water.
Spray neem oil (azadirachtin) to deter feeding and disrupt larval development.
Use pheromone or light traps to monitor and reduce adult populations.
Encourage natural enemies such as birds, ground beetles and parasitic wasps.
chemical_treatments: Apply a labelled insecticide such as carbaryl or a pyrethroid when beetle numbers exceed the economic threshold.
Soil-applied insecticides for root-feeding grubs where recommended.
Always follow the pre-harvest interval on the product label.
prevention: Practise crop rotation to break the beetle life cycle.
Remove crop residues and weeds that shelter beetles.
Use floating row covers on young vegetable crops.

damage_symptoms: Chewed leaf margins, large irregular holes, and defoliation.
Boring into fruits, pods, or stems (fruit borers, stem borers).
Presence of dark green or black droppings (frass) on leaves.
Rolled or webbed leaves where the larva shelters (leaf rollers).
organic_treatments: Hand-pick caterpillars and egg masses and destroy them.
Spray Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) — a biological insecticide highly effective on young larvae and safe for beneficials.
Apply neem oil to deter feeding and egg-laying.
Install pheromone traps to catch adult moths and time control measures.
Encourage parasitic wasps (Trichogramma) and predatory birds.
chemical_treatments: Use a labelled insecticide such as emamectin benzoate, spinosad, or chlorantraniliprole for heavy infestations.
Rotate insecticide groups to avoid resistance.
Spray in the evening when larvae are actively feeding.
prevention: Scout fields regularly for egg masses on the underside of leaves.
Remove weeds and crop residues that host larvae.
Time planting to avoid peak moth flight periods.

damage_symptoms: Earthworms are beneficial soil organisms — they do not damage crops.
They improve soil structure, aeration, drainage and nutrient cycling.
A high earthworm count is a sign of healthy, fertile soil.
organic_treatments: No treatment needed — protect and encourage earthworms.
chemical_treatments: None. Avoid excessive tillage and harsh chemical fertilisers/pesticides that harm earthworm populations.
prevention: Add organic matter (compost, mulch) to encourage earthworm activity.
Minimise deep tillage and avoid soil fumigants.

damage_symptoms: Small, irregular holes in leaves, petals and soft fruits, usually at night.
Damage to seedlings and tender shoots.
Note: earwigs are partly beneficial — they also eat aphids and insect eggs, so light populations can be tolerated.
organic_treatments: Set rolled-up damp newspaper or cardboard traps at dusk and destroy earwigs collected in the morning.
Shallow containers of vegetable oil or beer as pitfall traps.
Remove damp hiding places (mulch piles, boards) near seedlings.
Apply diatomaceous earth around vulnerable plants.
chemical_treatments: Spot-treat with a labelled insecticide bait only when seedling damage is severe.
prevention: Keep the area around seedlings dry and free of debris.
Protect young transplants with collars until established.

damage_symptoms: Ragged, chewed leaf edges and heavy defoliation in outbreaks.
Cut young shoots and can strip a plant rapidly when in large numbers.
Swarming locust forms can devastate entire fields.
organic_treatments: Encourage natural predators — birds, poultry, spiders and predatory wasps.
Apply the biopesticide Nosema locustae or Metarhizium (green muscardine fungus) where available.
Neem-based sprays deter feeding on young crops.
Till the soil after harvest to expose and destroy egg pods.
chemical_treatments: Apply a labelled contact insecticide (e.g., malathion or a pyrethroid) during heavy infestations or hopper bands.
Bait formulations with insecticide-treated bran for localised control.
prevention: Monitor field margins and grasslands where grasshoppers breed.
Keep weeds down to reduce egg-laying sites.
Coordinate area-wide control with neighbouring farms during outbreaks.

damage_symptoms: Adult moths themselves do not chew crops, but they lay eggs that hatch into destructive caterpillars.
Seeing many moths at night/around lights signals an incoming caterpillar generation.
Some (e.g., grain moths) infest stored produce.
organic_treatments: Use pheromone traps and light traps to catch adult moths before they lay eggs.
Remove and destroy egg masses on the underside of leaves.
Encourage bats, birds and parasitic wasps (Trichogramma) that attack moth eggs.
Apply Bt or neem to the crop to kill the caterpillars once eggs hatch.
chemical_treatments: Target the larval (caterpillar) stage with a labelled insecticide rather than spraying adults.
For stored-grain moths, use approved fumigation and airtight storage.
prevention: Monitor moth catches in traps to predict and pre-empt caterpillar outbreaks.
Store grain in sealed, clean containers.
Remove crop residues that harbour pupae.

damage_symptoms: Irregular holes with smooth edges in leaves and fruit, mostly on lower/inner leaves.
Silvery, slimy mucus trails on plants and soil — a tell-tale sign.
Seedlings can be cut off and destroyed overnight.
Most active at night and in damp, humid weather.
organic_treatments: Hand-pick at night or early morning and destroy.
Set beer traps (shallow dishes) to attract and drown slugs.
Sprinkle crushed eggshells, wood ash, or diatomaceous earth as barriers around plants.
Encourage natural predators — ducks, frogs, ground beetles and birds.
Use iron phosphate slug pellets, which are safe for pets and wildlife.
chemical_treatments: Metaldehyde molluscicide pellets applied sparingly around affected beds (follow label; keep away from children/pets).
prevention: Improve drainage and reduce excess moisture and dense mulch near stems.
Water in the morning so soil surface dries by night.
Clear hiding places — boards, stones, weeds and debris.

snail.scientific_name: Class Gastropoda (shelled); incl. golden apple snail Pomacea spp. in paddy
damage_symptoms: Irregular holes with smooth edges in leaves and stems; slime trails present.
Golden apple snails cut and eat young rice seedlings at the base in flooded paddies, causing missing hills.
Feed mostly at night and in wet conditions.
organic_treatments: Hand-pick snails and egg clusters (bright pink egg masses of apple snails on stems) and destroy.
Place attractant baits (papaya/banana leaves) and collect snails in the morning.
Make bamboo/screen barriers at water inlets to stop apple snails entering paddy.
Keep water level low (2–3 cm) during early rice establishment to reduce snail activity.
Encourage ducks (rice-duck farming), which eat snails.
chemical_treatments: Apply a labelled molluscicide (e.g., metaldehyde or niclosamide) at recommended rates in paddy where infestation is severe.
Follow label rates carefully — molluscicides can be toxic to fish.
prevention: Level paddy fields well and manage water depth to discourage snails.
Install screens at irrigation inlets.
Collect and destroy egg masses regularly during establishment.

damage_symptoms: Most wasps are beneficial — parasitic and predatory wasps kill caterpillars, aphids and other pests, providing natural control.
A few social wasps may nibble ripe/damaged fruit, but this is minor compared with their benefit.
Their main concern is stings near people, not crop damage.
organic_treatments: Generally no treatment needed — conserve wasps as natural enemies of pests.
Bag or net high-value ripe fruit if wasp feeding is a problem.
Remove only nests that pose a direct stinging risk to workers, ideally at night, with care.
chemical_treatments: Avoid broad-spectrum spraying, which kills these beneficial insects.
Treat only individual problem nests near work areas if strictly necessary.
prevention: Encourage parasitic wasps for biological pest control.
Harvest ripe fruit promptly and remove fallen/rotting fruit.

damage_symptoms: Adults chew small holes and notches in leaves and stems.
Larvae bore inside stems, roots, tubers or grains — hidden but very damaging.
Stored-grain weevils hollow out rice and maize grains, leaving light, powdery grain.
Banana/coconut weevils tunnel into the corm/trunk, weakening the plant.
organic_treatments: Use pheromone traps to monitor and mass-trap adults (e.g., banana/sweet-potato weevils).
Apply neem-based products to deter feeding and egg-laying.
Remove and destroy infested plant parts, tubers and crop residues.
For stored grain: sun-dry thoroughly, use airtight/hermetic storage, and mix in wood ash or neem leaves.
Encourage entomopathogenic nematodes/fungi (Beauveria bassiana) for soil-dwelling larvae.
chemical_treatments: Apply a labelled insecticide targeting adults during peak activity where thresholds are exceeded.
For stored grain, use approved grain protectants or fumigation in sealed stores.
Observe pre-harvest and storage safety intervals strictly.
prevention: Practise crop rotation and field sanitation to break the life cycle.
Use clean, weevil-free planting material and seed.
Dry grain to safe moisture (<14%) before airtight storage.

damage_symptoms: Small brown sap-sucking hoppers clustered at the base of rice plants, just above the water line.
Causes 'hopperburn' — circular patches of yellowing and drying plants that spread across the field.
Transmits rice viruses (grassy stunt, ragged stunt).
Sudden population explosions (resurgence) often follow misuse of broad-spectrum insecticides.
organic_treatments: Grow resistant/tolerant rice varieties recommended for your area.
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertiliser, which favours planthopper buildup.
Drain the field for 3–4 days to expose the plant base and reduce humidity at the base.
Conserve natural enemies — mirid bugs, spiders and wolf spiders; avoid spraying that kills them.
Apply neem-based products where infestation is starting.
chemical_treatments: Use a selective insecticide such as buprofezin or pymetrozine when numbers exceed the threshold.
AVOID broad-spectrum insecticides (synthetic pyrethroids) — they kill natural enemies and trigger worse resurgence.
Direct the spray at the base of the plants where hoppers feed.
prevention: Use recommended plant spacing and avoid dense, over-fertilised crops.
Synchronise planting with neighbours and keep a rice-free period to break the cycle.
Monitor the base of plants weekly and act early.

rice_stem_borer.scientific_name: Scirpophaga incertulas (yellow stem borer) / Chilo spp.
damage_symptoms: Caterpillars bore into the stem; the central shoot dies and dries — called 'deadheart' — during the vegetative stage.
At the flowering stage, panicles turn white and empty — called 'whitehead'.
Small bore holes on the stem and frass (droppings) inside.
Creamy-white egg masses covered with brown hairs on leaf tips.
organic_treatments: Clip and destroy leaf tips carrying egg masses; remove and destroy stubble after harvest.
Install pheromone traps to monitor and mass-trap adult moths.
Release the egg parasitoid Trichogramma where available.
Grow resistant varieties and avoid excess nitrogen.
Encourage natural enemies and use light traps for the moths.
chemical_treatments: Apply a labelled granular or spray insecticide such as cartap hydrochloride or chlorantraniliprole at the deadheart/early stage.
Time the application to the moth flight peak indicated by traps.
Follow the pre-harvest interval on the label.
prevention: Plough and flood fields after harvest to kill larvae in stubble.
Use certified, resistant planting material.
Synchronise planting across the area to avoid continuous host availability.

damage_symptoms: Young larvae scrape leaves leaving 'windowpane' patches; older larvae make ragged holes.
Larvae hide deep in the whorl of maize, leaving moist sawdust-like frass (droppings).
A dark inverted 'Y' mark on the head and four dots in a square on the second-to-last segment identify the larva.
Can bore into cobs and destroy growing points.
organic_treatments: Scout young plants twice a week; hand-pick and crush egg masses and larvae, and apply a pinch of dry sand/ash into the whorl.
Spray Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) on young larvae — effective and safe for beneficials.
Use pheromone traps to detect moths and time control.
Encourage natural enemies (parasitic wasps, birds, earwigs).
Apply neem-based products into the whorl.
chemical_treatments: Use a labelled insecticide such as spinosad, emamectin benzoate, or chlorantraniliprole directed into the whorl.
Rotate insecticide groups to prevent resistance.
Spray in the early morning or late evening when larvae are active.
prevention: Plant early and avoid staggered planting that provides continuous food.
Practise crop rotation with non-host crops.
Keep fields weed-free and monitor with pheromone traps from emergence.

damage_symptoms: Females puncture the fruit skin to lay eggs, leaving small 'sting' marks and oozing.
Maggots tunnel inside, causing the fruit to rot and drop prematurely.
Cut-open fruit shows white maggots and brown, decayed flesh.
Heavy losses near harvest time.
organic_treatments: Hang methyl-eugenol / pheromone traps to catch and monitor male flies (male annihilation technique).
Bag individual fruits with paper/net covers while they are still small.
Collect and destroy (bury deep or solarise) all fallen and infested fruit to break the cycle — sanitation is the single most important step.
Use protein bait sprays (a spot of yeast/protein hydrolysate + insecticide) to attract and kill females.
Harvest fruit slightly early where practical.
chemical_treatments: Apply spot bait sprays containing a labelled insecticide rather than full-cover sprays.
Cover-spray only if infestation is severe, following the label and pre-harvest interval.
prevention: Maintain strict orchard/field sanitation throughout the season.
Set up traps before fruits begin to ripen.
Coordinate trapping and sanitation with neighbouring growers for area-wide control.

damage_symptoms: Very tiny slender insects; rasp the leaf surface and suck sap, leaving silvery/whitish streaks.
Leaves and buds curl upward, crinkle and become distorted ('leaf curl' in chili).
Flowers and young fruit may be scarred or drop.
Important virus vectors (tospoviruses such as spotted wilt).
organic_treatments: Hang blue sticky traps to monitor and reduce adults.
Spray neem oil (azadirachtin), which disrupts thrips feeding and development.
Keep plants well-watered — thrips thrive under dry, stressed conditions.
Encourage predatory mites, minute pirate bugs and lacewings.
Remove weeds around the field that harbour thrips.
chemical_treatments: Use a labelled insecticide such as spinosad or fipronil, rotating groups to avoid resistance.
Add a wetting agent and aim spray into leaf whorls/undersides where thrips hide.
Observe the pre-harvest interval.
prevention: Use virus-free, healthy seedlings and reflective/silver mulch to repel thrips.
Avoid continuous cropping of the same susceptible crop.
Scout with sticky traps from early crop stages.

damage_symptoms: Soft insects covered in white, cottony wax, clustered in leaf axils, undersides, stems and on fruit.
Suck sap causing yellowing, leaf curl, stunting and fruit drop.
Excrete sticky honeydew that leads to black sooty mould on leaves and fruit.
Often tended and spread by ants.
organic_treatments: Prune and destroy heavily infested shoots and fruit.
Wash colonies off with a strong jet of water or a soap-water spray.
Spray neem oil or horticultural oil to smother them.
Control the ants that protect them (sticky bands on trunks) so natural enemies can work.
Release/encourage the mealybug destroyer beetle (Cryptolaemus) and ladybirds and parasitic wasps.
chemical_treatments: Use a labelled systemic insecticide only for severe infestations, as the waxy coat resists contact sprays.
Add horticultural oil to improve coverage and penetration of the wax.
Follow the label and pre-harvest interval.
prevention: Inspect and use clean, mealybug-free planting material.
Keep ant populations down around the crop.
Avoid excessive nitrogen and remove crop debris that harbours them.

damage_symptoms: Small green/brown wedge-shaped hoppers that jump/fly when disturbed; suck sap from leaves.
Cause yellowing, browning of leaf tips and margins ('hopperburn') and stunting.
Key vector of rice tungro virus and other plant diseases.
Honeydew and sooty mould may appear in heavy infestations.
organic_treatments: Grow resistant varieties and avoid excess nitrogen fertiliser.
Use yellow sticky traps and light traps to monitor and reduce adults.
Conserve natural enemies — spiders, mirid bugs and egg parasitoids.
Apply neem-based sprays at early infestation.
Maintain balanced water management in paddy.
chemical_treatments: Apply a labelled, need-based insecticide only when the action threshold is reached.
Avoid repeated broad-spectrum sprays that cause resurgence; rotate groups.
Direct spray to the lower canopy where hoppers feed.
prevention: Use tungro-resistant rice varieties in virus-prone areas.
Synchronise planting and keep a fallow/rice-free period.
Scout regularly with sticky and light traps.
